cards.name: Glaucoma
short: A progressive eye disease: the eye pressure rises and the optic nerve is damaged; the goal is to decrease the pressure. Open angle: the aqueous humor does not drain well, and there are no symptoms at first. Angle closure: tied to the shape of the eye, painful, an emergency.

Inflow is the making of aqueous humor by the ciliary body; outflow is its drainage. Decrease inflow: beta receptor antagonists, alpha 2 agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Increase outflow: M3 agonists, the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, prostaglandin agonists, the Rho kinase inhibitor.

Dr. Lam adds the classes in order from most to least commonly prescribed: prostaglandin analog (once daily), beta blocker, alpha-2 agonist, topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, cholinergic, Rho kinase inhibitor; the dosing frequency rises as the classes are added, and a higher frequency lowers adherence.

Between eye products wait 5 minutes (two solutions, or a solution then a suspension) or 10 minutes (before an ointment or gel). The order is solution, suspension, ointment or gel. Contact lenses come out first and go back in after 15 minutes.

After the drop, press the inner corner of the eyelid so less drug is absorbed into the body. The eye doctor measures the IOP, 2–4 weeks after a drug is started and every 3–4 months once the target is reached.

rows: A progressive eye disease. The pressure inside the eye, the [[iop|intraocular pressure (IOP)]], rises, and the {{optic nerve}} is damaged; vision is lost
{{Decrease the IOP}}, which delays or prevents disease progression

Usually {{gradual and asymptomatic}} until visual field loss occurs

The {{shape of the eye}} and how it sits in the eye socket (slide 13)
A {{medical emergency}}: the IOP must be decreased quickly

The slide ties it to the shape of the eye. In lecture the closed angle was also described as the outflow area closing after a blow to the eye with swelling, or a chemical exposure; the pressure rises very quickly and can damage the nerve

steps.title: Aqueous humor: inflow and outflow
steps.q: Where is aqueous humor made, by which two routes does it leave, and which receptors and enzyme sit in the ciliary body? How does a drug get into the eye?
steps.src: Eye slides 14–16; lecture 11/13; Sikazwe OOO slides 28–30; lecture 11/18; Eye slides 4, 7; lecture 11/13

rows: The [[ciliary-body|ciliary body]] (a ring behind the iris, with smooth muscle) makes [[aqueous-humor|aqueous humor]] all the time
Ciliary body → {{posterior chamber}} (between the lens and the iris)
Out of the anterior chamber through the {{angle}}
The {{drainage}} of aqueous humor out of the eye
Through the [[trabecular-meshwork|trabecular meshwork]], a spongy tissue
Most of the aqueous humor leaves this way
[[uveoscleral|Uveoscleral]] outflow: between the uvea and the sclera
If the aqueous humor does not drain, the pressure builds in the anterior chamber and is transferred toward the optic nerve, damaging it

blocks.text: Receptors and enzymes in the ciliary body and meshwork (slide 16)

rows: Blood vessels of the ciliary body
{{M3}} (muscarinic) receptors, and maybe some beta 2 receptors

items: How the receptors lead to aqueous humor is not fully known. The role of carbonic anhydrase is understood better.
Agonizing the beta receptors gave more aqueous humor; antagonizing them gave less. That led to the beta receptor antagonists.
Beta antagonists, alpha 2 agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors decrease the production of aqueous humor.

rows: Light is refracted through the lens and concentrated onto the retina, where the rods and cones are the light-sensing receptors
The colored part, in front of the lens
A clear tissue in front of the iris and lens that protects them; similar tissue to the sclera, but not opaque, and continuous with it
The firm white part that goes all the way around the eyeball
The nerves of the rods and cones are bundled into it; it sends the image to the brain
The tissue lining the eyeball, full of blood vessels, which supply the retina
Smooth muscle covered by epithelial tissue; a ring behind the iris around the lens. Suspension (zonular) ligaments hold the lens to it
The back part holds the gelatinous vitreous; the front part holds a less gelatinous liquid, the aqueous humor
Adrenergic stimulation of alpha 1 receptors dilates the pupil
Cholinergic stimulation of muscarinic receptors constricts the pupil
Cholinergic stimulation of muscarinic receptors contracts it, which increases accommodation; adrenergic stimulation relaxes the ciliary muscle for far vision and produces aqueous humor
She let the students read slides 7 and 8 and noted that eye doctors use these effects to dilate the eyes; her study hints say there is no need to memorize slides 8 or 9

blocks.text: How an eye drug gets in (Dr. Sikazwe, slides 28–30)

rows: The problem is raised IOP; the treatment goal is to {{decrease aqueous humor production}} or increase outflow, or both (slide 28)
A lipid / water / lipid sandwich: less drug enters (slide 29)
Influx and efflux transporters plus esterase and CYP enzymes: more drug enters (slide 29)
{{Lipophilic}} drugs enter through the cornea; the cornea is the main route for small lipophilic drugs (slide 30
{{Hydrophilic}} drugs enter through the conjunctiva; it is the main route for large hydrophilic drugs (slide 30
Conjunctival enzymes can bioactivate a prodrug placed in the eye (slide 29

steps.title: Treat it: does the drug decrease inflow or increase outflow?
steps.q: For each class, is it a production inhibitor or an outflow enhancer, and what does it act on? What functional group defines each class?

blocks.title: Inflow or outflow
rows: Decrease inflow (brimonidine also increases uveoscleral outflow)
Increase outflow, mainly uveoscleral; no effect on inflow
Increase outflow through the trabecular meshwork

blocks.label: Decrease inflow
blocks.title: Beta receptor antagonists
pts: Block the beta-adrenergic receptor on the ciliary body: {{less aqueous humor is made}}
{{Not much effect on outflow}}; the mechanism is not fully understood
Timolol, levobunolol, betaxolol, carteolol

blocks.label: Decrease inflow
blocks.title: Alpha 2 agonists
pts: Bind alpha 2 receptors on the ciliary body: {{decrease the rate of aqueous humor production}}
Brimonidine has two extra effects: it {{increases uveoscleral outflow}} and is {{neuroprotective}} (seen in animals)
pick: Preventing a rise in IOP after eye surgery such as cataract surgery

blocks.label: Decrease inflow
blocks.title: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
pts: Inhibit carbonic anhydrase: less carbonic acid, so less sodium and bicarbonate to secrete and {{less aqueous humor}}
Oral: acetazolamide, methazolamide. Ophthalmic: dorzolamide, brinzolamide
pick: The patient is refractory to other therapies
An oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor is added

blocks.label: Increase outflow
blocks.title: M3 agonists
pts: Agonize the M3 receptor on the sphincter muscle and the trabecular meshwork: they contract and {{outflow increases}}
Carbachol, pilocarpine
pick: Longer duration, less allergic reaction in the eye
More potential for an allergic reaction in the eye

blocks.label: Increase outflow
blocks.title: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor
pts: {{Irreversible}} inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase: more acetylcholine, the same contraction and increase in outflow
Used when a patient is refractory to other glaucoma medicines

blocks.label: Increase outflow
blocks.title: Prostaglandin agonists
pts: Agonize the {{PGF2α receptor}}: the ciliary muscle relaxes
Increase uveoscleral outflow and, to a lesser extent, trabecular outflow; they do {{not affect production}}
May be more effective in hazel or brown eyes than in blue or green eyes

blocks.label: Increase outflow
blocks.title: Rho kinase inhibitor
pts: Inhibits {{RhoA kinase}}: the trabecular meshwork relaxes (less stiff, fewer fibrosis-related proteins), so outflow increases

blocks.label: Two mechanisms
blocks.title: Combination products
pts: Timolol/dorzolamide, timolol/brimonidine, brinzolamide/brimonidine, latanoprost/netarsudil
Treatment often starts with one drug and moves to a combination as the disease progresses; one product replaces two

blocks.title: Chemical class of each drug group (Dr. Sikazwe)
rows: Aryl imidazoline core (slide 32, which is not on his assigned pages): the linker atom decides the receptor, X = NH gives alpha 2 agonists and X = CH2 gives alpha 1 agonists; the slide prints the linker as NH2, and the slide 31 structures show NH
Clonidine (ClogP 1.5) is lipophilic enough to enter the brain and cause CNS effects; brimonidine (ClogP 1.2) is about 1,000-fold more potent, so a tiny drop works (lecture 11/18)
{{Aryloxypropanolamines}}: timolol, betaxolol, levobunolol, carteolol (slide 33): an aromatic ring, the oxygen next to it, and three carbons carrying the alcohol and the amine (lecture 11/18)
More potent than the arylethanolamines; most have mixed beta 1 and beta 2 activity; the S-OH isomers are preferred; most para aryloxypropanolamines such as betaxolol are beta 1 antagonists (slide 34)
Carbonic anhydrase is a Zn-metalloenzyme that modulates aqueous humor production through pH changes: CO2 + H2O gives carbonic acid (H2CO3), which gives bicarbonate (HCO3-) and H+ (slide 35)
The SO2NH2 group forms ionic and hydrogen bonds with the zinc and Thr199 of the enzyme (slide 38)
Brinzolamide and dorzolamide both undergo CYP N-deethylation; the N-deethylated metabolites are active (slide 37)
{{Carbamates and esters}}: acetylcholine (ester), carbachol (carbamate), pilocarpine (slide 40). He told the class not to expect a question on the slide 40 SAR (lecture 11/19)
Extent of inhibition by functional group: {{phosphoryl > carbamate > ester}} (slide 42)
Echothiophate is an organophosphate and is irreversible: aging, the loss of an ethyl group, leaves a hydroxy group covalently bound to the enzyme (lecture 11/19)
A cyclopentane ring with an alpha chain and an omega chain; they raise outflow by activating the PGF (FP) receptor (slides 44, 46)

At C-1, acids and amides are active and esters are prodrugs; C-15 is OH or a halogen (slide 46). Bimatoprost is the amide; latanoprost, travoprost, tafluprost and latanoprostene bunod are esters that esterase converts to the acid (slides 44–46)
Omidenepag isopropyl: a pyridine sulfonamide, a selective EP2 receptor agonist and an ester prodrug that esterase activates; outflow increases (slide 47)

Netarsudil: an isoquinoline and an ester prodrug that esterase activates; outflow increases (slide 48). Dr. Smith's slides give outflow only; Dr. Lam's handout lists three effects: increased aqueous humor outflow, decreased aqueous humor production and decreased episcleral venous pressure
Question 3 (slide 65): the key functional group in the chemical basis of action of the carbonic anhydrase inhibitors is the sulfonamide
Question 4 (slide 66): the drawn imidazoline is present in the alpha 2 agonists
Question 5 (slide 67): the drawn core is the prostaglandin skeleton, present in the prostaglandin receptor agonists; the slide leaves the answer blank and he answered it in class (11/19)
Question 5, second part (slide 68): the phosphoryl group gives irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition (lecture 11/19)

Imidazoline, sulfone, sulfonamide, aryloxypropanolamine, carbamate, ester, the prostaglandin skeleton (cyclopentane with two chains) and the steroid skeleton. His emailed practice question 2 asks for the key functional groups of the anti-glaucoma classes drawn by hand; question 3 asks for the N-deethylated products of brinzolamide and dorzolamide

steps.title: Side effects, and what to tell the patient
steps.q: Which side effect goes with each class, why does a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor cause metabolic acidosis, and what lowers systemic absorption?

blocks.title: Side effect to know for each class
rows: Systemic: bradycardia, hypotension; bronchospasm in asthmatics (beta 2 blocked). Ocular: stinging, burning, decreased night vision
Allergic reaction (slide 24 lists it under systemic side effects; in lecture she called it significant, lecture 11/13); systemic hypotension (slide 24)
Foreign body sensation and itching of the eyes; oral dryness, dizziness, fatigue, somnolence, lower blood pressure and pulse
Oral: {{metabolic acidosis}}, increased urination, dry mouth, thirst, altered taste and smell, depression. Ocular drops: burning, stinging, bitter taste

blocks.text: ★ Why a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor causes metabolic acidosis (kidney, proximal tubule)

rows: Carbonic anhydrase makes carbonic acid, which splits into {{hydrogen ion}} and {{bicarbonate}}
Leaves the cell in exchange for sodium coming in
Leaves with sodium into the blood and {{buffers the blood pH}}
No carbonic acid, so no hydrogen ion to exchange for sodium: sodium and water stay in the lumen (more urine). No bicarbonate reaches the blood
The blood pH falls: {{metabolic acidosis}}, most important with the oral drugs
No bicarbonate is made in the ciliary body cells, so it is not secreted, water does not follow, and aqueous humor decreases

items: ★ After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid: the drug then does not drain through the tear duct into the nose, whose lining is highly vascularized, and is not absorbed into the bloodstream
Some glaucoma drops have cardiovascular effects, and older patients with glaucoma may already have heart conditions
For a cardiac patient on a beta receptor antagonist: a more selective drug, or the eyelid compression

blocks.label: First
blocks.title: Prostaglandin analogs
pts: Why first: once daily dosing gives better adherence; up to 33% IOP reduction meets the 25–30% goal; low-cost generics; good tolerance (slide 20
More than once daily decreases the efficacy, so a BID prescription is an error to fix with the prescriber; handout)

Blurred vision is the reason for nightly dosing; other side effects are stinging, increased pigmentation of the iris or eyelashes, eyelash growth and thickening, and a foreign body sensation (slide 21)
Contraindications: macular edema; history of herpetic keratitis. She said she will not test them (slide 21
pick: Change the formulation (solution to gel), switch to another class, or for a reaction to the preservative use a preservative-free product (slide 22)
Latanoprost (Xelpros) or tafluprost (Zioptan) (handout). She said she will say in the stem when a product is preservative-free

Check compliance and administration technique, and switch to another agent (slide 23); switch within the class or add another agent, and bimatoprost is slightly more effective, so it is the switch when latanoprost does not work (handout)
blocks.move: Move to the next class when: the response is partial and the drug is tolerated; the beta blocker is added.

blocks.label: Next
blocks.title: Beta blockers
pts: Decrease aqueous humor production; 20–30% IOP reduction, less than the prostaglandin analogs (slide 31; handout)
BID; timolol gel (Timoptic-XE) is once daily: fewer doses a day and fewer systemic effects than the solution (slide 32; handout)
Betaxolol is less effective than timolol and levobunolol; the suspension (Betoptic-S) has fewer systemic effects than the solution (handout)
Local: stinging on application (especially betaxolol solution), dry eyes, blepharitis, blurred vision. Systemic: bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm (slide 33)

Precautions: asthma or COPD; bradycardia or 2nd or 3rd degree heart block; uncompensated cardiac failure; oral beta-blocker therapy; less risk with betaxolol and carteolol (slide 34; handout). She said the precaution concerns uncontrolled disease. She said she will not test the incidence of bronchospasm
pick: Change the formulation (solution to gel); switch agent or class (betaxolol to timolol); for a preservative reaction use a preservative-free product, for example Cosopt PF or certain timolol products (slide 35)
Ensure compliance; increase the concentration if possible; if one agent does not work, switch to another class (slide 36)
Timolol solution to Timoptic XE gel, 1 drop once daily (slides 32, 37

blocks.label: Next
blocks.title: Alpha-2 agonists
pts: Handout: increase outflow and decrease production; 18–27% IOP reduction; also used for surgical purposes, 1 drop before the procedure
Brimonidine (Alphagan P) BID; apraclonidine (Iopidine) BID or TID, with a higher incidence of side effects that stop on discontinuation (slide 42; handout)

Local, most common: lid edema, eye discomfort, foreign-object sensation, itching. Systemic: dizziness, fatigue, somnolence, dry mouth, slight blood pressure or heart rate change; the handout lists drowsiness as most common and a blood pressure change under 10% (slide 43)
Precautions: cardiovascular and kidney disease, history of stroke, certain drugs; the handout names antihypertensives, MAO inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants (slide 44)

{{Lumify}} (brimonidine 0.025%) is OTC for ocular redness and is not for glaucoma; it is not a therapeutic substitute for prescription brimonidine, because it is not efficacious enough to reduce the IOP (slides 42, 47
pick: Reduce the concentration if possible; decrease the frequency (apraclonidine only); switch to another class (slide 45)
Ensure compliance; increase the concentration if possible; add the next class (slide 46)

blocks.label: Then
blocks.title: Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
pts: TID; 15–26% IOP reduction; the reduction is smaller and the frequency higher than the earlier classes (slide 51

Local: stinging or burning that resolves within 1–2 minutes, ocular discomfort, blurred vision as the drop settles, tearing; systemic effects minimal (slide 52; handout. Stinging that lasts longer than that goes to the ophthalmologist

Oral acetazolamide and methazolamide (25–40%): short-term use only, because of systemic acidosis (malaise, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, weight loss, altered taste). She said to know that the oral drugs cause systemic acidosis and are last line; Dr. Smith's detail on how acidosis occurs she would not test, though she did not guarantee it (slide 53
Precautions: sickle cell disease, pulmonary disorders, electrolyte imbalance; sulfonamide allergy, where cross-sensitivity is very low (slide 54). She called the cross-sensitivity an FYI
pick: Switch from topical to oral; switch to another class; for a preservative reaction a preservative-free product (Trusopt preservative-free, in the handout: certain brand names only) (slide 55)
Ensure compliance; switch to another agent in the class or add another therapy; switch from topical to oral (slide 56)

blocks.title: Cholinergic agonists (miotics)

Rarely used, because of the IOP reduction and the four-times-a-day dosing. The handout adds that pilocarpine may be used as initial management of acute angle-closure glaucoma
Local: poor night vision, frontal headache or brow ache, stinging. Systemic: headache (the most common), sweating, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramping, bronchospasm, heart block (slide 58)
Precautions: asthma; retinal detachment or corneal abrasion (slide 59)
pick: Reduce the concentration if possible; switch to a drug in a different class (slide 60)
Ensure compliance; increase the concentration if possible; add another agent (slide 61)

steps.q: What do you tell the patient about the bottle, the eyelid, the waits, the order, contact lenses and storage, and when does the eye doctor check the pressure?

cards.name: Allergic conjunctivitis
short: Antigen binds IgE on a [[mast-cell|mast cell]]; histamine is released and causes itching, swelling and redness. Itching is the sign that separates allergic conjunctivitis from bacterial or viral conjunctivitis.

First line (Dr. Lam): artificial tears plus an OTC ophthalmic dual-acting agent (antihistamine and mast cell stabilizer). Ophthalmic antihistamines are H1 inverse agonists; most also stabilize mast cells; cetirizine does not.
Decongestants (alpha 2 agonists) reduce redness only, and are limited to 72 hours. An oral second-generation antihistamine is added when the ophthalmic products do not work.
Refer when pain, trauma, chemical exposure, heat exposure, blurred vision, light sensitivity or eyelid infection is present, or when there is no benefit after 72 hours of appropriate treatment.
Order of application: solution, suspension, ointment or gel; wait 5 minutes between solutions and 10 minutes before a gel; contact lenses out, back in after 15 minutes.

cards.name: Dry eye
short: [[ksc|Keratoconjunctivitis sicca]]: inflammation reduces tear production; common, with age and female gender as risk factors. It feels sandy or gritty, and the eye is normal or mildly red.

Dr. Lam: refer every patient with a first episode to an eye doctor; OTC artificial tears can be used while waiting. Exclusions: eye pain, trauma, chemical or heat exposure, blurred vision, light sensitivity, eyelid infection.
Find and remove the cause (dry air, screens, offending drugs). Artificial tears first line, with no set duration; a bland ointment or gel is the longer-lasting step, and it blurs vision.
Prescription drugs are not first line: cyclosporine (about 6 months), lifitegrast (about 12 weeks), a topical corticosteroid (very short term), varenicline nasal spray (about 4 weeks).

Cyclosporine: a calcineurin inhibitor; blocks IL-2 production. Lifitegrast: blocks LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1; contact lenses out before the drop, back in after 15 minutes. Varenicline: a nicotinic receptor agonist that increases tear production.

Mucins, from the {{goblet cells}} in the conjunctiva
Nutrients, enzymes and immunoglobulins that support and protect the cornea

Nicotinic receptor agonist: activates the trigeminal parasympathetic pathway; more basal tear film

{{1 drop}} in each eye {{twice daily}}, about every 12 hours

{{One spray in each nostril}} twice daily, about 12 hours apart

beta-blockers.name: Beta receptor antagonists (timolol, levobunolol, betaxolol, carteolol)

sm.text: Block the beta-adrenergic receptor on the ciliary body, so less aqueous humor is made (inflow falls); not much effect on outflow; the mechanism is not fully understood. Timolol and levobunolol: nonspecific beta blockers (levobunolol has some alpha-adrenergic effects). Betaxolol: relatively beta 1 selective. Carteolol: nonspecific with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. Side effects: ocular stinging and burning, decreased corneal sensitivity, diplopia, blurred or cloudy vision, decreased night vision, ptosis; systemic bradycardia and hypotension, bronchospasm in asthmatics, headache, insomnia, taste perversion, depression, impotence.

counsel: After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.
Timolol comes as a gel that is given once a day; the other drops are given several times a day.
Effectiveness is similar across the group; the choice can rest on side effects or insurance coverage.
Local side effects (stinging, dry eyes, blepharitis, blurred vision) are a major counseling point. With an oral beta blocker, check the blood pressure and heart rate, especially when it is started.
A patient who forgets the evening dose can be changed from timolol solution to the once-daily gel.

Cardiac patients: bradycardia and hypotension (slide 20); a more selective drug, or the eyelid compression (11/13)
Levobunolol may be more effective than timolol and betaxolol after cataract surgery (11/13)
Asthma or COPD; bradycardia or 2nd or 3rd degree heart block; uncompensated cardiac failure; oral beta-blocker therapy; less risk with betaxolol and carteolol (Lam Glaucoma slide 34)

la.text: Timolol 0.25% and 0.5% (Timoptic, Istalol): 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes twice daily. Timoptic-XE gel: once daily (fewer doses a day, fewer systemic effects than the solution). Betaxolol (Betoptic 0.5%, Betoptic-S 0.25%), carteolol 1% (Ocupress), levobunolol 0.25% and 0.5% (Betagan): twice daily. Betaxolol is less effective than timolol and levobunolol; the Betoptic-S suspension has fewer systemic effects than the solution. Combinations: timolol with dorzolamide (Cosopt, Cosopt PF) and with brimonidine (Combigan), both twice daily. IOP reduction 20–30%.

sk.text: Aryloxypropanolamines (an aromatic ring, the oxygen next to it, then three carbons carrying the alcohol and the amine): timolol maleate (Timoptic, Log P 1.4), betaxolol HCl (Betoptic, 2.5), levobunolol HCl (Betagan, 2.2), carteolol HCl (Ocupress, 1.4). They decrease aqueous humor production. SAR: more potent than the arylethanolamines; most have mixed beta 1 and beta 2 activity; the S-OH isomers are preferred; most para aryloxypropanolamines such as betaxolol are beta 1 antagonists.

apraclonidine.name: Apraclonidine

sm.text: An alpha 2 agonist: binds alpha 2 receptors on the ciliary body and decreases aqueous humor production (inflow). Used to prevent a rise in IOP after eye surgery such as cataract surgery; not used long term because of an allergic type response. Side effects: ocular burning and stinging, blurred vision, foreign body sensation, ocular pruritus; systemic hypotension, oral dryness, allergic reaction.

la.text: Apraclonidine 0.5% and 1% (Iopidine): 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes twice or three times daily; also used for surgical purposes, 1 drop before the procedure. Higher incidence of side effects, which stop on discontinuation. Intolerance: decrease the frequency (this applies only to apraclonidine).

sk.text: Apraclonidine HCl (Iopidine, ClogP 0.87) is clonidine plus an aromatic amino group; it is less lipophilic than clonidine (ClogP 1.5), so it does not enter the brain as well and the CNS effects of clonidine are avoided.

brimonidine.name: Brimonidine

sm.text: An alpha 2 agonist: binds alpha 2 receptors on the ciliary body and decreases aqueous humor production (inflow). Two extra effects: it increases uveoscleral outflow and is neuroprotective (seen in animals, assumed in humans). The better choice for long-term glaucoma treatment. Side effects: foreign body sensation and itching of the eyes (a hallmark); systemic oral dryness, dizziness, fatigue, somnolence, lower blood pressure and pulse. For allergic conjunctivitis: an alpha 2 agonist vasoconstrictor that reduces redness (brimonidine tartrate).

pa.how: Brimonidine tartrate is on the list with naphazoline, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline and phenylephrine.

counsel: Glaucoma: After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.
Allergic conjunctivitis: it constricts the blood vessels in the eye, which reduces redness.
Prescription brimonidine for glaucoma is not replaced by OTC Lumify (0.025%), which is for redness.
brimonidine.counselSrc: Eye slides 56–57; lecture 11/13; lecture 11/17; Lam Glaucoma slide 47; lecture 11/19
avoid: Foreign body sensation and itching of the eyes are the notable ocular effects (11/13)

la.text: Alphagan P solution, various concentrations: 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes twice daily. Combinations: with timolol (Combigan) twice daily; with brinzolamide (Simbrinza) three times daily. Lumify 0.025% is OTC for ocular redness only: it is not for glaucoma and is not a substitute for prescription brimonidine (0.1% in her case; the handout gives 0.1%–0.2% for the prescription strength), because it is not efficacious enough to reduce the IOP. IOP reduction 18–27%.

sk.text: Brimonidine tartrate (Alphagan products, ClogP 1.2): a bromine-bearing benzo-fused pyrazine joined to the imidazoline through NH; alpha 2 selective and the most potent of the series, about 1,000-fold more potent than clonidine, so a tiny drop in the eye works with little worry about brain entry.

cai.name: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, methazolamide, dorzolamide, brinzolamide)

sm.text: Inhibit carbonic anhydrase, which prevents the conversion of CO2 and water to carbonic acid; less sodium and bicarbonate are available for secretion, so the ciliary body makes less aqueous humor (inflow falls). Acetazolamide and methazolamide are oral; dorzolamide and brinzolamide are ophthalmic. Side effects of the drops: burning or stinging, hypersensitivity, headache, bitter, sour or unusual taste, dry eye, foreign body sensation, blurred vision. Oral: altered taste and smell, dry mouth, excessive thirst, increased urination, systemic acidosis, depression.

The ophthalmic product comes first; an oral drug is added if the patient is refractory to other therapies.
Stinging or burning right after the drop is common and resolves within 1–2 minutes; stinging that lasts longer goes to the ophthalmologist. Blurred vision is the drop settling.
Oral acetazolamide and methazolamide are short-term only: systemic acidosis (malaise, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, weight loss, altered taste).
cai.counselSrc: lecture 11/13; lecture 11/17; Lam Glaucoma slides 52–53; handout; lecture 11/19
avoid: Oral use: metabolic acidosis; the blood pH must be watched (11/17)
Oral use: over-diuresis can show as dry mouth and thirst (11/17)
Sickle cell disease, pulmonary disorders, electrolyte imbalance; sulfonamide allergy, where cross-sensitivity is very low (Lam Glaucoma slide 54; she called it an FYI, lecture 11/19)

la.text: Topical: dorzolamide 2% (Trusopt) and brinzolamide 1% suspension (Azopt), 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes three times daily; shake the suspension. Combinations: dorzolamide/timolol (Cosopt, Cosopt PF) twice daily; brinzolamide/brimonidine (Simbrinza) three times daily. IOP reduction 15–26% topical, 25–40% oral. Oral acetazolamide and methazolamide: short-term use only, because of systemic acidosis. Stinging or burning lasts 1–2 minutes; blurred vision is the drop settling.

sk.text: Sulfonamides (zolamides) that competitively inhibit carbonic anhydrase, a Zn-metalloenzyme that modulates aqueous humor production through pH changes (CO2 + H2O gives H2CO3, then HCO3- and H+). ClogP: acetazolamide -0.3, methazolamide 0.13, dorzolamide HCl 2, brinzolamide 7 (the first-generation agents are polar, oral and high dose; the second-generation agents are lipophilic, topical and small dose). The SO2NH2 group forms ionic and hydrogen bonds with zinc and Thr199. Brinzolamide and dorzolamide both undergo CYP N-deethylation, and the N-deethylated metabolites are active. His practice question 3 asks for those two metabolites drawn.
sk.src: Sikazwe OOO slides 35–38; lecture 11/18; practice question 3

m3-agonists.name: M3 agonists (carbachol, pilocarpine)

sm.text: Direct-acting parasympathomimetics: agonists at the M3 receptor on the sphincter muscle and the trabecular meshwork; contraction increases outflow. Carbachol is very potent and longer acting, and is used more often; pilocarpine has more potential for an allergic reaction in the eye. Side effects: burning and stinging; painful ciliary muscle spasm causing headache; blurred vision, myopia, poor vision in dim light, floaters, lacrimation; systemic diarrhea, salivation, sweating, rhinorrhea.

Systemic cholinergic effects (diarrhea, salivation, sweating, rhinorrhea) come from drug absorbed through the nose; the compression lowers this.

la.text: Pilocarpine 1%, 2% and 4% (Isopto Carpine): 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes four times daily; the handout says it may be used as initial management of acute angle-closure glaucoma. Carbachol (Miostat) is often used for surgery instead of glaucoma. Rarely used for glaucoma because of the IOP reduction and the four-times-a-day dosing. Local: poor night vision (pupil constriction), frontal headache or brow ache, stinging. Systemic: headache, sweating, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramping, bronchospasm, heart block.

sk.text: Direct-acting cholinergics are carbamates and esters: acetylcholine (ester), carbachol Cl (carbamate; weak indirect effects) and pilocarpine HCl raise fluid outflow. SAR on the slide: acyloxy group for hydrogen bonding to the nicotinic or muscarinic receptors, an ionizable amine, N-methyl groups, a 2-carbon spacer between O and N. He told the class not to expect a question on this SAR.

avoid: Asthma; retinal detachment or corneal abrasion (Lam Glaucoma slide 59)

echothiophate.name: Echothiophate

sm.text: An irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: more acetylcholine agonizes the M3 receptors, the sphincter muscle and trabecular meshwork contract, and outflow increases. Used when a patient is refractory to other medicines. Side effects: burning and stinging, blurred vision, eye pain, lacrimation, headache, brow ache, twitching of the eyelids, an allergic type reaction (more than pilocarpine), cataracts; systemic diarrhea, salivation, sweating, rhinorrhea.

how.text: An irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: more acetylcholine agonizes the M3 receptors, the sphincter muscle and trabecular meshwork contract, and outflow increases. Used when a patient is refractory to other medicines. Side effects: burning and stinging, blurred vision, eye pain, lacrimation, headache, brow ache, twitching of the eyelids, an allergic type reaction (more than pilocarpine), cataracts; systemic diarrhea, salivation, sweating, rhinorrhea.

counsel: After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.
avoid: Can cause cataracts, a reason its use is limited in patients who already have glaucoma (11/17)

la.text: Echothiophate has many serious ocular and systemic toxic effects (severe fibrinous iritis in the handout); it is in the class of cholinergic agonists, the fifth class she adds.

sk.text: An organophosphate (phosphoryl group): the extent of acetylcholinesterase inhibition is phosphoryl > carbamate > ester. It is irreversible: with time the enzyme-drug bond ages, an ethyl group is lost and a hydroxy group leaves the enzyme covalently and irreversibly bound; the antidote must be given before aging. It is the only drug working in this fashion. His self-assessment question 5 asks which functional group shows irreversible inhibition.

pg-agonists.name: Prostaglandin agonists (bimatoprost, latanoprost, latanoprostene bunod, travoprost, tafluprost)

sm.text: Agonists at the PGF2α receptor, which relaxes the ciliary muscle; IOP falls by increasing uveoscleral outflow and, to a lesser extent, trabecular outflow. They do not affect aqueous humor production. May be more effective in hazel or brown eyes than in blue or green eyes. Latanoprostene bunod is also a nitric oxide donor (vasodilation adds to its effect). Side effects: blurred vision, burning and stinging, eye pain, lid edema, ocular hyperemia; increased brown pigmentation of the iris and eyelids; hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation of the lashes (Latisse); hair growth in other areas; few systemic effects.

counsel: Expect darker pigmentation of the iris and eyelids and longer, thicker lashes.
After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.
Give it in the evening: blurred vision is the reason for nightly dosing. Do not give it more than once a day, because a higher frequency decreases the effect.
pg-agonists.counselSrc: Eye slide 39; lecture 11/17; Lam Glaucoma slides 20–21; lecture 11/19

la.text: Bimatoprost 0.01% and 0.03% (Lumigan), latanoprost (Xalatan, Xelpros), latanoprostene bunod (Vyzulta, a prodrug of latanoprost), travoprost (Travatan Z), tafluprost (Zioptan): 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes once daily, in the evening; more than once daily decreases the efficacy. IOP reduction up to 33%. Latisse (bimatoprost) is for eyelash hypotrichosis (the handout prints 0.03%, slide 19 prints 0.3%). Storage: latanoprost, latanoprostene bunod and tafluprost in the refrigerator before opening, room temperature once opened. Preservative-free: latanoprost (Xelpros) and tafluprost (Zioptan).

sk.text: A cyclopentane ring with an alpha chain and an omega chain; activation of the PGF (FP) receptor raises outflow. At C-1, acids (COOH) and amides (CONH) are the active drugs and esters are prodrugs that esterase converts to the acid (latanoprost isopropyl ester to latanoprost acid); C-15 is OH or a halogen (halogens prevent oxidation of the 15-OH). Bimatoprost is the amide; latanoprost, travoprost, tafluprost and latanoprostene bunod are esters; tafluprost carries two fluorines.

avoid: Macular edema; history of herpetic keratitis (Lam Glaucoma slide 21; she will not test them, lecture 11/19)

netarsudil.name: Netarsudil

sm.text: Inhibits RhoA kinase. RhoA is a GTP-binding protein that regulates cell shape, motility, proliferation and apoptosis; in glaucoma it may increase contractile tone and trabecular meshwork stiffness. Inhibiting it lowers outflow resistance (outflow only on Dr. Smith's slides): it relaxes the tone, decreases fibrosis-related protein deposits in the meshwork and changes the permeability of the cells lining Schlemm’s canal. The only Rho kinase inhibitor on the drug list. Side effects: conjunctival hyperemia (53%), from vasodilation; about 20%: corneal verticillata (vision unchanged, resolved on stopping in most cases), instillation site pain, conjunctival hemorrhage.

counsel: Red eyes (conjunctival hyperemia) are common; the cause is relaxation of vascular smooth muscle.
After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.

la.text: Netarsudil 0.02% (Rhopressa): 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes once daily in the evening; with latanoprost it is Rocklatan, once daily in the evening. IOP reduction 20–30%, like timolol. Mechanism in her handout: increased aqueous humor outflow, decreased aqueous humor production and decreased episcleral venous pressure (Dr. Smith's slides give outflow only). Refrigerate before opening; once opened, room temperature for less than 6 weeks. Conjunctival hemorrhage or hyperemia was reported in 51% (handout; it is last-line because the side effect outweighs the efficacy.

sk.text: An isoquinoline Rho kinase (ROCK) inhibitor that raises fluid outflow. It is an ester prodrug: esterase hydrolysis gives the active metabolite netarsudil-M1. ClogP 5.

glaucoma-combos.name: Glaucoma combination products

sm.text: Timolol and dorzolamide; timolol and brimonidine; brinzolamide and brimonidine; latanoprost and netarsudil. Treatment often starts with one drug and moves to a combination as the disease progresses. One product with both mechanisms replaces two bottles.

how.text: Each product joins two of the mechanisms above: a beta receptor antagonist, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, an alpha 2 agonist, a prostaglandin agonist or the Rho kinase inhibitor.

counsel: A drop that has to be used 3 or 4 times a day is easier to follow as one combination product than as two separate drops.
After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.
A patient who has trouble waiting between many drops can use a combination product, so one bottle replaces two.
glaucoma-combos.counselSrc: lecture 11/17; lecture 11/13; Lam Glaucoma slides 69, 76–81; lecture 11/19

la.text: Brimonidine/timolol (Combigan): alpha-2 agonist and beta blocker, twice daily. Dorzolamide/timolol (Cosopt, Cosopt PF): carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and beta blocker, twice daily. Brinzolamide/brimonidine (Simbrinza): carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and alpha-2 agonist, three times daily. Netarsudil/latanoprost (Rocklatan): once daily in the evening. She said to recognize the classes in each product and its dosing. Her 11/20 email corrects slide 51: Simbrinza is brinzolamide and brimonidine.

ophthalmic-h1.name: Ophthalmic H1 inverse agonists (antihistamines)

sm.text: H1 inverse agonists: reduce the constitutive activity of the receptor and compete with histamine for it. Most also stabilize mast cells, which reduces the release of mast cell mediators and is anti-inflammatory (less cytokine secretion, less adhesion molecule expression, inhibition of eosinophil infiltration). Mast cell stabilization may make them more effective topically. They reduce edema, itch, inflammation and watery eyes. Examples: alcaftadine, azelastine, bepotastine, cetirizine, epinastine, ketotifen, olopatadine; cetirizine has no mast cell stabilization.

counsel: A drug with mast cell stabilization can be started before the allergen season to prevent the release of histamine.
Cetirizine is not the one to suggest for prophylactic use: it has no mast cell stabilization, and it can still cause drowsiness.

la.text: OTC dual-acting agents: olopatadine (Pataday, Patanol), alcaftadine 0.25% and ketotifen fumarate 0.025%; prescription: azelastine, bepotastine and epinastine, each twice daily. Relief begins within minutes, up to 30 minutes. They can be used when symptoms are present or chronically, and before the season starts because preventing mast cell degranulation takes time. First line is artificial tears plus one of them.

sk.text: Not on his assigned pages (his Exam 3 readings end at slide 48): the dual-acting agents are multi-cyclic with ionizable N and COOH groups; the SAR is not clearly stated.

alcaftadine.name: Alcaftadine

sm.text: H1 inverse agonist with mast cell stabilization, and H4 receptor antagonism (H4 is on eosinophils; this may explain its superiority in allergic conjunctivitis). Very little anticholinergic activity, little CNS penetration, low incidence of side effects.

how.text: H1 inverse agonist with mast cell stabilization, and H4 receptor antagonism (H4 is on eosinophils; this may explain its superiority in allergic conjunctivitis). Very little anticholinergic activity, little CNS penetration, low incidence of side effects.

la.text: OTC: alcaftadine 0.25%, 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes once daily; relief within 3 minutes; ages 2 years and older. (Dr. Smith's drug chart lists alcaftadine, Lastacaft, as Rx; Dr. Lam lists it as OTC.)

counsel: Once daily, 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes; relief begins within 3 minutes.
For ages 2 years and older.

epinastine.name: Epinastine

sm.text: H1 inverse agonist with mast cell stabilization. Also an H2 antagonist, which may reduce eyelid edema.

how.text: H1 inverse agonist with mast cell stabilization. Also an H2 antagonist, which may reduce eyelid edema.

la.text: Prescription dual-acting agent (recognize): 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes twice daily; she rarely sees it dispensed.

sk.text: Not on his assigned pages (slide 57): a multi-cyclic dual-acting agent (Elestat).

counsel: Prescription; 1 drop in the affected eye or eyes twice daily.

cetirizine-eye.name: Cetirizine (ophthalmic)

sm.text: H1 inverse agonist without mast cell stabilization. Minimal anticholinergic effects and negligible CNS penetration, but it still causes drowsiness.

how.text: H1 inverse agonist without mast cell stabilization. Minimal anticholinergic effects and negligible CNS penetration, but it still causes drowsiness.

counsel: It is the ophthalmic antihistamine not suggested for prophylactic use, because it has no mast cell stabilization.

la.text: Cetirizine 0.24%: for mild allergic conjunctivitis; it only blocks histamine receptors, so it is not a dual-acting agent. It relieves itching and redness for a limited time and needs frequent dosing, up to four times a day (handout and her speech); the handout also gives 1 drop twice daily about 8 hours apart. No systemic adverse effects; prolonged use may cause eye irritation.

sk.text: Not on his assigned pages (slides 53–54): cetirizine (Zerviate) is a 2nd-generation H1 antihistamine; the SAR is deferred to the allergy lecture.

naph-pheniramine.name: Naphazoline/pheniramine

sm.text: An alpha 2 agonist (vasoconstrictor, reduces redness) combined with an H1 antihistamine; one drop instead of two covers both approaches.

how.text: An alpha 2 agonist (vasoconstrictor, reduces redness) combined with an H1 antihistamine; one drop instead of two covers both approaches.

la.text: Pheniramine maleate/naphazoline (Naphcon-A, OTC): 1–2 drops in the affected eye or eyes up to 4 times a day. Side effects: pupil dilation (anticholinergic properties), burning, stinging. She said many OTC eye products are combinations, so read the active ingredient.

sk.text: Not on his assigned pages (slides 53–54): pheniramine maleate (in Opcon-A) is a first-generation H1 antihistamine with a pyridine ring, a phenyl ring and a dimethylamino group.

counsel: 1–2 drops up to 4 times a day; it can dilate the pupil and cause burning and stinging.
It contains a decongestant as well as an antihistamine, so read the active ingredients of each OTC eye product.

alpha2-eye.name: Alpha 2 agonist vasoconstrictors (naphazoline, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline, brimonidine tartrate, phenylephrine)

sm.text: Adrenergic receptor agonists: vasoconstrictors for local application to the nasal mucous membrane or the eye. They reduce redness, and less leaking from the capillaries reduces edema. Little difference between them for allergic conjunctivitis.

how.text: Adrenergic receptor agonists: vasoconstrictors for local application to the nasal mucous membrane or the eye. They reduce redness, and less leaking from the capillaries reduces edema. Little difference between them for allergic conjunctivitis.

la.text: Decongestants: naphazoline (OTC), tetrahydrozoline (Visine, OTC), brimonidine 0.025% (Lumify, OTC). They reduce ocular redness as local vasoconstrictors and do not diminish the allergic response. Dosing: generally four times a day, for up to 72 hours. Beyond 72 hours: rebound conjunctival hyperemia, allergic blepharitis, possible angle-closure glaucoma, epithelial xerosis. They can raise the blood pressure through systemic absorption. She said to recognize which drugs are decongestants, and that Lumify at this strength is not for glaucoma.

sk.text: Not on his assigned pages (slides 52 and 55): slide 55 prints the imidazoline decongestants with the mechanism of action line a1/a2 - agonists: Oxymetazoline HCl (Afrin products), Xylometazoline HCl (Clear eyes products), Tetrahydrometazoline HCl (Visine products) and Naphazoline HCl (Otrivin products). Slide 52 lists phenylephrine among the decongestants.

counsel: Use for about 72 hours at most: they reduce redness only; later use causes rebound redness and other problems.
They can raise the blood pressure; take care with hypertension, cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

cyclosporine.name: Cyclosporine

sm.text: Binds cyclophilin; the complex inhibits calcineurin, so IL-2 is not made for T-cell proliferation. Topical cyclosporine increases tear production where it is suppressed by ocular inflammation from keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Side effects: ocular burning, instillation site pain, conjunctival hyperemia, discharge, epiphora, eye pain, foreign body sensation, pruritus, stinging, visual disturbances.

artificial-tears.name: Artificial tears (ocular lubricants)

how.text: Products vary by viscosity: a higher viscosity gives a longer contact time and better resistance to tear dilution. Buffering agents, preservatives and pH also vary.

la.text: First line for dry eye. 1–2 drops once or twice a day, typically on waking and before bed; severe cases can use 3–4 times a day up to hourly. May be continued with no set limit, depending on the response. Preservative-free is preferred for moderate to severe dry eye or a patient sensitive to preservatives. In allergic conjunctivitis they wash out the allergen and protect the ocular surface, and they are part of first line with a dual-acting agent.

ophthalmic-ointment-gel.name: Bland ophthalmic ointment or gel

The gel causes less blurry vision than the ointment and is better tolerated. In the order of application an ointment or gel-forming product goes last, at least 10 minutes after drops.

iop: The pressure inside the eyeball. In glaucoma it increases, and over time it can damage the optic nerve.
aqueous-humor: The liquid the ciliary body makes all the time. It fills the anterior chamber and drains out of the eye through the angle.
ciliary-body: A ring behind the iris, with smooth muscle and blood vessels. It holds the lens by ligaments and makes the aqueous humor.
trabecular-meshwork: A spongy, porous tissue around the opening of Schlemm’s canal. Most aqueous humor leaves through it into the canal, and then the veins.
uveoscleral: The smaller outflow route: aqueous humor squeezes between the uvea (ciliary body, its ligaments and the iris) and the sclera.
mast-cell: A cell that stores histamine in granules. Antigen interacting with IgE on its surface releases the histamine.
inverse-agonist: The activity a receptor has on its own. An inverse agonist reduces it, and also competes with the natural ligand (histamine at H1).
mcs: Reduces the release of mast cell mediators during an allergic response and is anti-inflammatory. How it works is still unclear.
ksc: The name for dry eye: inflammation with reduced tear production.
cyclophilin: The protein cyclosporine binds; the cyclosporine–cyclophilin complex inhibits calcineurin.
lfa-1: Lymphocyte function-associated antigen 1: a cell surface protein on leukocytes that interacts with ICAM-1.
bak: The most common preservative in multi-dose eye drops; it causes ocular irritation in some patients, and contact lenses trap it against the surface of the eye.
dual-acting: Her short name for an ophthalmic antihistamine, mast cell stabilizer and histamine type 1 receptor antagonist in one drop.
xerosis: Abnormal dryness of the surface of the eye.
